title: ‘I’m Really Terrified’: A Mathematician Grapples With AI’s Recent Breakthroughs
gist: Cornell mathematician Steven Strogatz argues that OpenAI's tens-of-thousands-of-agents assault on a 90-year-old Navier-Stokes problem and Anthropic's 29,500-theorem Fermat formalization are primarily marketing instruments in a race to grab headlines ahead of blockbuster IPOs, not research with end-user value. He predicts breakthrough mathematics becomes impossible without AI, that human roles compress to proof digestion and taste, and that funding for human mathematicians is the first economic casualty.

themes.theme: AI lab capability race and its scoreboard

insights.claim: OpenAI deployed tens of thousands of agents to solve a 90-year-old mathematics problem carrying a $1 million prize, with the solution still requiring independent verification and building on a strategy developed by Spanish mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Massive parallel agent deployment against a single verifiable target is now a demonstrated capability pattern — read it as a compute-consumption signal as much as a research result.
insights.locator: On Tuesday, OpenAI said it had used tens of thousands of agents

insights.claim: Anthropic said Claude proved 29,500 small theorems while formalizing an existing proof that other mathematicians had been working on for years, and OpenAI announced advances on 10 other long-standing mathematical problems in August.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Formal-verification throughput is becoming the head-to-head benchmark between frontier labs; expect it in fundraising and IPO narratives.
insights.locator: Last week, Anthropic said Claude had proved 29,500 small theorems

insights.claim: The current burst of mathematical announcements is best explained as corporate labs racing to grab headlines ahead of blockbuster IPOs rather than as demand-driven research.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: If announcement cadence is IPO-timed, treat capability headlines as sell-side marketing and discount them accordingly when modeling actual deployed value.
insights.locator: The rupture is a symptom of the rapid changes

insights.claim: The Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem has essentially no interest to working civil or aerodynamic engineers and matters only to a tiny subset of pure mathematicians, making the solution a marketing device to demonstrate machine quality rather than a commercially useful result.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A frontier-lab benchmark win with zero end-market demand should not be extrapolated into near-term revenue; separate proof-of-capability from proof-of-product.
insights.quote: It doesn't affect anybody except it's maybe worth a trillion dollars for OpenAI to show they're better than Anthropic.
insights.locator: On the significance of solving the Navier-Stokes

insights.claim: The perceived competitive value of showing superiority over a rival lab on a single arcane problem is framed as being worth on the order of a trillion dollars, implying capability leadership is priced into valuation rather than into cash flow.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Narrative leadership, not utility, is the currency in this cycle — watch for the moment benchmark wins stop moving private valuations.
insights.locator: This is a marketing device for them

insights.claim: Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster alleges that OpenAI rushed to solve the problem after learning of his work with an Anthropic researcher, and that OpenAI also tried to influence who received credit for the result.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Attribution disputes between labs and academics are an emerging reputational and possibly legal risk category for AI companies courting scientific legitimacy.
insights.locator: The announcement was marred by claims

insights.claim: Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge posted solutions to three closely related and slightly easier problems a couple of days before OpenAI's announcement, creating a genuine dispute over who should receive the million-dollar prize.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Near-simultaneous human and machine results suggest the problem was ripe regardless of AI, weakening claims that the agent swarm was the decisive factor.
insights.locator: Arguably, you could say Buckmaster should get the money

insights.claim: The visible human cost of AI-accelerated discovery includes researchers losing the career motivation that came from being first, with a senior collaborator saying he feels his 15 years of research training and peak skill have been surpassed and that he is now merely the one holding an AI agent.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Talent-retention risk in AI-exposed knowledge work shows up as demotivation before it shows up as headcount cuts; relevant to any firm whose moat is elite human expertise.
insights.quote: I'm the one with an AI agent, which feels very different actually. And I feel totally threatened by it.
insights.locator: I actually feel kind of upset that I've dedicated 15 years

insights.claim: Competing at the frontier of mathematical research will be impossible without AI going forward.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Implies universal, non-discretionary AI tooling spend across research institutions — a durable subscription demand floor independent of hype cycles.
insights.quote: You will not be able to compete without AI in the future if you want to do breakthrough math
insights.locator: “I think the year 2026 is going to be remembered

insights.claim: A decades-old numerical linear algebra problem was solved with help from ChatGPT, and the researchers said the volume of work and cost-reward ratio would have made the project unfeasible without the technology.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: The real economic mechanism is unlocking projects previously below the cost-benefit line, not replacing existing work — that expansion of addressable problems is where research-tool revenue actually accrues.

insights.claim: 2026 will be remembered as a decisive year for mathematics, characterized as either an annus mirabilis or an annus horribilis because of how much has happened in a compressed period.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A named inflection year gives a reference point for dating the start of AI-driven discovery in formal domains.
insights.locator: “I think the year 2026 is going to be remembered

insights.claim: The remaining human advantage is proof digestion — explaining machine-generated results in terms other humans can understand — but that role is expected to be surpassed by machines soon as well.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Interpretation and translation layers are the last defensible human niche in formal domains, and even that is a short-duration moat; price the option accordingly.
insights.quote: We need proof digestion, which is explaining it in terms that human beings can understand and appreciate.
insights.locator: On whether AI still needs human mathematicians

insights.claim: Disciplines that deal with the messy real world — economics, international relations, sociology — will be relatively resistant to AI displacement for longer than pure mathematics, because messiness itself is the barrier.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A usable ordering rule for AI displacement risk across knowledge sectors: formalizable and verifiable falls first, ambiguous and context-dependent last.
insights.quote: Applied math is messy because it deals with the real world. The messier the subject gets, the more resistant it will be to AI.

insights.claim: Machines have so far shown no sign of mathematical taste — the ability to judge which of infinitely many possible results are interesting to humans — but there is no structural reason they could not be trained on aesthetic questions to acquire it.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Taste and problem-selection is the next benchmark frontier after raw solving; whoever demonstrates it credibly captures the next narrative cycle.
insights.quote: So who will be the arbiter of good mathematical taste?
insights.locator: You could do infinitely many things in math

insights.claim: If mathematics becomes a recreational pursuit at which humans are permanently second-rate, the justification for paying human mathematicians disappears, and that is described as a very possible trajectory absent intervention.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Research funding reallocation away from human headcount toward compute is a concrete budget shift to watch in university and grant flows.
insights.quote: If that's all that math is, then why would anyone pay us to do it?
insights.locator: It could be, but that has a lot of implications

insights.claim: AI in mathematics is simultaneously devastating and democratizing — the questions specialists loved are being answered without them, while participation opens to people who never completed the traditional decades of training.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: The same dynamic hits any credentialed profession: incumbent rent compression plus entrant expansion, which usually favors tooling platforms over incumbent gatekeepers.
insights.quote: Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.
insights.locator: On what AI means for math

insights.claim: Mathematics is framed as the first battleground where humanity stands on the brink of losing understanding of results produced on its behalf, with mathematicians serving as the canary in the coal mine for other domains.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Verification and interpretability of machine output becomes a societal requirement, creating demand for audit and formal-verification tooling well beyond math.
insights.quote: I feel like we're the first battleground here in math where we're on the brink of losing human understanding
insights.locator: On what it means for humanity
